title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials
authors: Lucas Fourel, Paul Devianne, Marine Debouvry, Tristan Destruhaut, Russell Gunn, Ashwini Gupta
abstract: Computational homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations of heterogeneous materials require repeated solution of mechanical fields on Representative Volume Elements, which becomes prohibitively expensive for high-resolution three-dimensional microstructures. Machine-learning surrogates can accelerate these computations, yet most existing approaches predict fields for fixed macroscopic loadings and provide limited guidance on how to scale network architectures for high-resolution 3D tensor-field prediction. This work presents a U-Net surrogate trained to predict the full 36-component strain localization tensor field in voxelized concrete mesostructures at resolutions up to $256^3$. Training localization tensors are generated with an FFT-based linear elastic solver, and an extensive hyperparameter optimization is performed to derive scaling rules and an accuracy-speed trade-off analysis. The results show that only network width and depth need to be scaled with problem complexity, while several conventional U-Net design choices, such as doubling channels after downsampling, are suboptimal for this problem. The final neural network achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 1.118% on both the validation and the held-out test sets, and an inference speedup of approximately 8.7x over the FFT-based solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU. Generalization experiments reveal transfer across aggregate volume fractions and highlight the importance of training on diverse morphologies. To safeguard reliability, a Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric computed on internal feature maps is proposed for detecting out-of-distribution microstructures without costly reference computations.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D U-Net predicts full 36-component strain localization tensor fields by scaling network width and depth, while conventional channel-doubling is suboptimal for this task.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate could accelerate repeated mechanical-field calculations in concrete homogenization and coupled multiscale simulations.
method: Train on voxelized concrete mesostructures up to 256³ using localization tensors from an FFT-based linear elastic solver.
Optimize U-Net architecture to derive scaling rules and accuracy–speed trade-offs.
Use Maximum Mean Discrepancy on internal feature maps to flag out-of-distribution microstructures without reference solves.
infographic.evidence_signal: The final model reports 1.118% mean absolute error on both validation and held-out test sets, approximately 8.7× inference speedup over the FFT solver on an Nvidia H100 GPU, and transfer across aggregate volume fractions.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization depends on morphological diversity in training; out-of-distribution detection is a warning mechanism, not an accuracy guarantee.
infographic.paper_title: Neural network scaling and generalization for 3D strain fields in heterogeneous materials

title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
authors: Megha Srivastava, Michael H. Lim, Allison M. Keys, Pranav Murugan, Nate Gruver
abstract: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-guided feature discovery ranks protein–ligand poses more accurately than direct LLM reasoning, reaching up to 74% accuracy on Pyrite.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated pose ranking could help drug-discovery teams prioritize candidate binding geometries generated by cofolding models.
method: Build PyriteRep to encode molecular geometry, protein–ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores.
Compare direct pose reasoning with LLM-generated features used in logistic regression.
Apply Group Relative Policy Optimization to improve open-weight models.
infographic.evidence_signal: On a benchmark of 1,500 pose pairs, PyriteReasoner and PyriteFeaturizer achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, while tool-equipped expert chemists perform near chance.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark ranking accuracy does not establish prospective drug-discovery value; generalization to new targets and pose-generation pipelines needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents

title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
authors: Hadi Salloum, Ammar Ali
abstract: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.

infographic.key_insight: Tree-Ising repairs reasoning loops through sparse BF16 weight edits, outperforming an LLM-agent repair without gradients or LLM tokens.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Discrete weight optimization offers a low-cost repair workflow using four forward-pass requests and about $0.90 in GPU time for the annealing recipe.
method: Use forward statistics to weaken looping, strengthen concluding, and preserve productive-token outputs.
Restrict edits to admissible sign flips and exponent shifts while preserving shared group exponents and mantissas.
Decompose the objective exactly into per-row QUBO problems solved with GPU simulated annealing or simulated bifurcation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Qwen3.5-0.8B, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6–55.1% MATH-500 accuracy versus 51.7% for the agent edit; improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K remain significant after multiple-comparison correction.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the reported Qwen models and math benchmarks; the eight-variable QAOA demonstration does not establish practical quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits

title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
authors: Bo Dai, Yilun Du
abstract: Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

infographic.key_insight: Energy-based models provide a unifying lens for machine learning through three choices: energy function, inference procedure, and learning method.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This framework suggests new algorithms by swapping components and combining learned energies at inference time.
method: Define distributions as pθ(x) ∝ exp(−Eθ(x)), with energy determining what the model represents.
Connect sampling, variational inference, and learning objectives through a shared contrastive structure.
Map generative, discriminative, representation-learning, reinforcement-learning, and verifier-based methods into the same framework.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a conceptual tutorial spanning many model families, but reports no datasets, quantitative benchmarks, or empirical comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Practical tractability depends on how each formulation handles the partition function and sampling.
infographic.paper_title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning

title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
authors: Ziang Liu, James J. Kim, Yijia Dai, Jennifer J. Sun
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

infographic.key_insight: Contrastive Discovery helps scientific agents identify which competing explanation evidence supports, rather than merely reject a single hypothesis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Existing discovery agents can adopt contrast sets to reinterpret collected evidence or guide experiments without increasing the experiment budget.
method: Pair each scientific question with mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive explanations.
Score experiments by how evidence redistributes belief across those explanations.
Resolve a question when belief concentrates on one explanation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six domains, contrast sets resolved 73% of high-belief-shift pointwise rejections to specific alternatives; guided search resolved 67% more questions, while 38 blinded experts agreed with 78% of resolved answers.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on constructing genuinely exhaustive, nonoverlapping explanation sets; omitted alternatives could produce misleading confidence.
infographic.paper_title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations

title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)
authors: Ziqing Xu, Hancheng Min, Lachlan Ewen MacDonald, Salma Tarmoun, Enrique Mallada, Weijie Su
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. These properties are central to continual and multi-task learning, yet remain poorly understood. In this work, we provide a theoretical explanation through a unified \textit{margin-based perspective}. We analyze LoRA in multiclass linear classification under a near-orthogonal task regime with $\ell_2$-regularization, and characterize the optimal LoRA adapter across regularization regimes. Our analysis shows that, in an intermediate regime of regularization parameters, the optimal adapter aligns with the \emph{max-margin solution} on the fine-tuning data. Building on this characterization, we derive two key consequences. First, we obtain closed-form expressions for the margins on pre-training and fine-tuning data, revealing a precise margin trade-off: the regularization parameter controls the balance between retention and adaptation. Second, we analyze adapter merging, proving that merged models achieve positive margin on each task and deriving optimal mixing coefficients that balance margins across tasks and maximize the margin over their union. These results lead to a simple, training-free merging rule, which we term \textit{margin-based LoRA merging} (MaLoRA). Experiments on modern architectures and real datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that MaLoRA matches or outperforms several adapter-merging baselines across a range of vision and language classification tasks.

infographic.key_insight: A margin-based analysis links LoRA’s resistance to catastrophic forgetting and mergeability, motivating MaLoRA’s training-free adapter-merging rule.
infographic.engineering_relevance: MaLoRA offers a principled way to combine task-specific LoRA adapters using mixing coefficients designed to balance task margins.
method: Analyze multiclass linear LoRA under near-orthogonal tasks and ℓ₂ regularization.
Show max-margin alignment at intermediate regularization and quantify the retention–adaptation trade-off.
Derive merge coefficients that maximize the minimum margin across tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on modern architectures and real vision and language classification datasets report MaLoRA matching or outperforming several adapter-merging baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Theoretical guarantees rely on a linear, near-orthogonal task setting; applicability to nonlinear models with strongly overlapping tasks needs validation.
infographic.paper_title: A Margin Perspective on LoRA: Robustness to Catastrophic Forgetting and Adapter Merging (MaLoRA)

title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models
authors: Dong Han, Jin Zhang, Kunyue Yang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly exhibit capabilities that resemble human Learning by Thinking (LbT), the acquisition of new insight through internal processes such as explanation and reasoning, without new external input. A systematic account of the cognitive mechanisms behind these capabilities, and of their limits, remains underdeveloped. This paper proposes a Cognitive LbT Framework that maps four mechanisms (Reflective Reasoning, Synthetic Memory Formation, Internal Simulation, and Conceptual Self-Organization) onto computational processes in LLMs. Drawing on representative methods, including chain-of-thought prompting, self-consistency, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts search, Self-Instruct, and self-taught reasoning, the analysis argues that selected methods can functionally approximate aspects of these mechanisms and can improve performance on some tasks without additional labeled examples, although this does not always constitute durable learning in model parameters. For example, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33% absolute improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions (Y. Wang et al., 2023). The same mechanisms also produce characteristic failures, including hallucination diffusion, model collapse, concept drift, and high computational cost. These failures are not isolated technical defects but follow from four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition: the identity of generator and monitor, closed learning loops without external grounding, symbolic rather than sensorimotor simulation, and the cost of inference-time computation. The framework yields testable propositions about when LbT in LLMs should succeed or fail and offers a structured basis for designing more reliable autonomous learning systems.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed cognitive framework maps four ways LLMs can approximate learning by thinking while linking their failure modes to structural differences from human cognition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers design hypotheses for more reliable autonomous learning systems by distinguishing inference-time gains from durable parameter learning.
method: Map reflective reasoning, synthetic memory formation, internal simulation, and conceptual self-organization onto LLM processes.
Analyze representative methods, including chain-of-thought, self-reflection, Tree-of-Thoughts, and Self-Instruct.
Connect characteristic failures to four structural asymmetries between LLMs and human cognition.
infographic.evidence_signal: As a cited example rather than a new experiment, Self-Instruct generated approximately 52,000 instructions from 175 seed tasks and reported a 33-percentage-point improvement on Super-NaturalInstructions.
infographic.watch_item: Closed, ungrounded self-learning loops can propagate hallucinations or model collapse, and improved task performance need not imply durable learning.
infographic.paper_title: Cognitive Mapping of Learning by Thinking Mechanisms in Large Language Models

title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation
authors: Yu Dong, Hong Li, Qiang Sun, Xu Zhou, Jinbiao Huo, Qixiu Cheng
abstract: Evaluating candidate parallelization strategies through distributed training runs makes strategy selection prohibitively expensive at scale. Performance simulation offers a lower cost alternative, yet controlled comparisons among existing simulators remain difficult because they differ in the training stages they model and the workloads on which they are evaluated. We introduce LM-SimBench, a unified framework, profiling dataset, and benchmark for evaluating LLM training simulators. The framework decomposes simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule level aggregation, connecting execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets. Following this framework, we profile 23 model settings from 10 dense and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) LLM families on an Ascend Neural Processing Unit (NPU) cluster. The resulting dataset contains 348 feasible configurations that jointly vary five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation, with six views spanning configuration, rank, operator, event, and kernel granularity. Evaluations of representative training simulators demonstrate how LM-SimBench supports comparisons of prediction accuracy, assessment of configuration selection, and diagnosis of prediction errors. Matched GPU-NPU experiments validate the cross-platform applicability of the collection and evaluation protocol and demonstrate NPU-guided GPU configuration selection.

infographic.key_insight: LM-SimBench unifies LLM training simulation evaluation so researchers can compare prediction accuracy, configuration selection, and error sources across simulators.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation can reduce reliance on costly distributed training trials when selecting parallelization strategies.
method: Decompose simulation into functional stages from model compilation to schedule-level aggregation.
Connect execution representations and cost estimators to measurable evaluation targets.
Profile workloads across five parallelism dimensions and activation recomputation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset covers 348 feasible configurations across 23 model settings from 10 dense and MoE LLM families on an Ascend NPU cluster, with representative simulator evaluations and matched GPU–NPU experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Cross-platform experiments support applicability, but prediction accuracy and configuration rankings should be validated on target hardware and workloads.
infographic.paper_title: LM-SimBench: A Unified Framework, Dataset, and Benchmark for Large Language Model Training Simulation

title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing
authors: Naveen Babu Narayanan Nair, Sajay Kurup
abstract: Software agents built on large language models generate traffic unlike human web traffic, yet routers have no class for it and cannot verify a sender's claim to be an agent. This paper proposes the Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class (VATC), which combines a reserved Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) value declaring agent traffic, a router-side classifier that demotes flows contradicting the declaration to a class served after best-effort traffic, and a rate-limited priority queue. VATC was compared with static Differentiated Services (DiffServ), a dedicated class that trusts the marking, and fq_codel, a per-flow fair-queuing scheduler, in two simulators and on a real Linux kernel. VATC matched DiffServ under steady load. In a constructed burst it cut mean agent queuing delay by 98% relative to DiffServ in simulation (assuming an immediate verdict), at a 12% increase in human delay; most of the gain came from the separate class. Under a spoofed flood in the kernel, the rate limit held human latency 11 times below DiffServ's. Without verification, DiffServ and a tightly configured fq_codel gave legitimate agents lower latency than VATC; a live four-feature classifier then demoted all 20 bulk-shaped spoofers and gave agents 0.30 ms, but missed six spoofers that copied the agent pattern. With emulated network delay, a timing feature of the classifier stopped separating agent from human flows. In real agent harnesses on a congested link, router queueing took 13% to 63% of task time, depending on harness and assumed model latency. The traffic was synthetic or sandbox-scale.

infographic.key_insight: VATC combines declared agent traffic, router-side verification, and rate-limited priority scheduling to reduce agent queuing delay while protecting human traffic from spoofed floods.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Network engineers could use VATC to prioritize latency-sensitive AI agents, but benefits depend on classifier reliability and careful queue configuration.
method: Mark agent traffic with a reserved DSCP value.
Demote flows that contradict their agent declaration to below best-effort service.
Serve accepted agent traffic through a rate-limited priority queue.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two simulators and Linux-kernel tests, VATC cut mean agent queuing delay 98% versus DiffServ in a constructed burst assuming immediate verification, increased human delay 12%, and kept human latency 11 times below DiffServ under a spoofed flood.
infographic.watch_item: Results used synthetic or sandbox-scale traffic; the live classifier missed six agent-pattern spoofers, and emulated network delay erased one timing feature’s ability to distinguish agents from humans.
infographic.paper_title: Verifiable Agentic Traffic Class: A Policed Quality-of-Service Mechanism for Agentic AI Traffic, Evaluated from Simulation to Real-Kernel Adversarial Testing

title: Beyond Accuracy: Physics-Informed Evaluation of ANN-based Power Flow Solvers under System Shift
authors: Dong Liu, Jochen Stiasny, Jochen Cremer, Pedro P. Vergara
abstract: Recent advances in artificial deep learning-based power flow (PF) solvers have primarily focused on improving estimation accuracy, while their physical feasibility and operational reliability under realistic system variations remain insufficiently evaluated. This paper proposes a physics-informed evaluation framework for deep learning-based PF solvers under topology and load distribution shifts. Beyond conventional voltage-domain errors, the framework incorporates KCL gaps, branch-flow gaps, KVL residuals, continuous feasibility scores, and strict, practical, and relaxed PF feasibility rates. Four case studies are designed to investigate topology shifts, mixed topology training, load distribution shifts, and combined topology distribution shifts. Eight ANN architectures, including graph input models, load-only baselines, and physics-informed neural networks, are evaluated under consistent settings. The results demonstrate that low estimation errors do not necessarily correspond to physically feasible or operationally reliable PF solutions, particularly under combined system shifts. The proposed framework establishes an initial foundation and analysis for the development and verification of trustworthy deep learning-based PF solvers, providing support for their reliable deployment in future AI-enabled power system analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Low voltage-prediction errors do not necessarily imply physically feasible or operationally reliable neural power flow solutions under system shifts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physics-based checks can help engineers assess neural power flow solvers beyond accuracy before deployment under changing grid topologies and load distributions.
method: Evaluate topology shifts, load distribution shifts, mixed-topology training, and combined shifts.
Measure KCL gaps, branch-flow gaps, KVL residuals, and continuous feasibility scores.
Report strict, practical, and relaxed power flow feasibility rates alongside voltage-domain errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight ANN architectures, including graph-input models, load-only baselines, and physics-informed neural networks, are evaluated under consistent settings across four case studies.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical feasibility results or threshold definitions, limiting assessment of deployment readiness.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Accuracy: Physics-Informed Evaluation of ANN-based Power Flow Solvers under System Shift

title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout
authors: Karol Struniawski
abstract: During extended wakefulness, mammalian neocortical networks experience localized periods of transient neuronal silence termed off-states. Here, we examine how analogous spatiotemporally concentrated disruptions affect sequential reasoning in autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating 250 paired derivations on the GSM8K benchmark across two 8B models (Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct), we contrast clustered bursts of attention head masking against budget-matched diffuse i.i.d. dropout. Concentrated bursts induce substantial reasoning degradation: at onset parameter $\mathcal{B}=0.10$ (scheduling $\sim 5.7\%$ of vulnerable head-token volume), Qwen3-8B accuracy drops from $91.2\%$ under diffuse noise to $78.8\%$ under burst dropout ($Δ= -12.4$ percentage points [pp], exact McNemar $p = 5.5 \times 10^{-6}$), while LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct drops from $84.0\%$ to $76.8\%$ ($Δ= -7.2$ pp, $p = 0.0198$). Conversely, dispersing the identical cumulative budget uniformly across generation steps via stratified quintile matching yields substantially milder degradation (retaining $91.2\%$ in Qwen and $84.0\%$ in LLaMA). In an exploratory factorial dissociation ($N=100$), single-step dropout density is associated with an acute drop in a single schedule draw ($-10.0$ pp on Qwen, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.0425$), while multi-token continuity exhibits an inconclusive compounding trend ($-7.0$ pp, $p_{\text{holm}} = 0.1892$). Error analysis reveals that Qwen failures reflect derivation errors within formatted responses (conditional accuracy drop of $-11.4$ pp), whereas in LLaMA $22.2\%$ of discordant losses lack a final answer format line (conditional gap narrows to $-5.0$ pp). These findings demonstrate that autoregressive reasoning chains are particularly vulnerable to concentrated structural disruptions, providing empirical benchmarks for fault tolerance in transformer architectures.

infographic.key_insight: Concentrated attention-head dropout disrupts autoregressive reasoning more than diffuse dropout with the same cumulative masking budget.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fault-tolerance testing for transformer inference should assess disruption concentration, not just overall dropout rates.
method: Evaluated 250 paired GSM8K derivations in Qwen3-8B and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct.
Compared clustered attention-head masking with budget-matched diffuse dropout and stratified temporal redistribution.
Explored single-step density versus multi-token continuity in a separate 100-example factorial evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: At onset parameter B=0.10, scheduling approximately 5.7% of vulnerable head-token volume, burst versus diffuse dropout reduced accuracy from 91.2% to 78.8% in Qwen (−12.4 pp; p=5.5×10⁻⁶) and from 84.0% to 76.8% in LLaMA (−7.2 pp; p=0.0198).
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to two 8B models on GSM8K; the exploratory continuity effect was inconclusive, and some LLaMA losses involved missing final-answer formatting.
infographic.paper_title: Breakdown of Autoregressive Multi-Step Reasoning Under Concentrated vs. Diffuse Attention Head Dropout

title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows
authors: Kaiyuan Hou, Yang Ping Kuo, Indranil Bhattacharya, Rohith Nama, Arushi Gupta, Carlos D. Castillo
abstract: Business process automation runs the same Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) again and again on new inputs. Large Language Model (LLM) agents can follow an SOP written in natural language, but they call an LLM to choose every step of every run, which adds latency and cost at scale. We present ReTrace, which turns an SOP and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow in which code, not an LLM, selects the next step. The agent's reasoning, the explanation it writes with each tool call, often states why it took an action; the tool calls alone do not. ReTrace extracts the condition behind each step, merges these conditions across runs into a compact rule document, and generates an executable workflow from it. Only this last stage depends on the platform, so rule documents can be compiled for different orchestration platforms. On $79$ procedures from our production platform, ReTrace workflows reach $93.8\%$ completion, against $96.8\%$ for the agent, at $24\%$ lower cost per task. On $τ^2$-Bench, they reach $75.8\%$ task success (agent: $80.6\%$) and run in $1.3$s instead of $170$s; three rounds of repair on training failures lift $k{=}2$ workflows from $66.7\%$ to $81.2\%$. On eight SOP-Bench procedures, ReTrace without repair trails few-shot generation ($80.6\%$ vs. $83.6\%$), but repair from labeled training failures lifts it to $87.8\%$ at $0.40$s per task, compared to $85.5\%$ in $46.6$s for the agent.

infographic.key_insight: ReTrace distills tool-using agents into reusable workflows where code selects each step, eliminating per-step LLM planning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Repeated SOP execution can become faster and cheaper, with platform-independent rule documents compiled into platform-specific workflows.
method: Extract action conditions from an SOP and reasoning in a few logged agent runs.
Merge conditions across runs into a compact rule document and generate executable workflows.
Optionally repair workflows using labeled training failures.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 79 production procedures, ReTrace achieved 93.8% completion versus the agent’s 96.8% at 24% lower cost; on τ²-Bench, it achieved 75.8% success versus 80.6% while running in 1.3 seconds versus 170 seconds.
infographic.watch_item: Unrepaired workflows can underperform agents or few-shot generation; reported repair gains rely on training failures, labeled for SOP-Bench.
infographic.paper_title: ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows

title: Cross-Border Fulfillment Center Selection via Doubly Robust Estimation and Linear Programming
authors: Kriti Mahajan, Patrick Bloebaum
abstract: We introduce the cross-border (XB) fulfillment center (FC) Selection Model: a multi-stage optimization framework combining forecasting, doubly robust estimation, and linear programming to select optimal source FCs. For each source-destination shipping arc, the objective is to choose a subset of source-country FCs that minimize delivery time and cost while maximizing profit and shipped units under a fixed domestic network. We evaluate the model on three production-scale international shipping corridors for a large e-commerce company using 12 months of shipment data, employing both aggregate offline replay and shipment-level counterfactual nearest-neighbor matching. Across all shipping corridors, the XB FC Selection Model achieves 8.5-51.1% reductions in delivery time and 4.4-48.3% reductions in logistics cost relative to human expert-defined FC selection policies, with up to 6.5 percentage-point improvements in 5/5 target compliance (5 days, $5 USD). Pareto analysis shows the model consistently dominates single-objective ranking strategies and unconstrained LP on the efficiency-reallocation frontier, with all results statistically significant.

infographic.key_insight: Combining doubly robust estimation with linear programming selects cross-border fulfillment centers that reduce delivery time and logistics cost versus expert-defined policies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports multi-objective fulfillment routing while keeping the domestic network fixed.
method: Forecast cross-border shipment demand.
Use doubly robust estimation to inform source-center selection.
Apply linear programming to balance delivery time, cost, profit, and shipped units.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three production-scale corridors using 12 months of data, offline replay and shipment-level counterfactual matching showed 8.5–51.1% faster delivery, 4.4–48.3% lower logistics cost, and up to 6.5 percentage-point gains in 5-day/$5 target compliance.
infographic.watch_item: Offline counterfactual evaluation does not establish live operational gains; prospective validation is needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Cross-Border Fulfillment Center Selection via Doubly Robust Estimation and Linear Programming

title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces
authors: Jiahang Lin, Wanying Ren, Wanghan Xu, Huayu Sha, Yang Shu, Zhonghang Lu
abstract: Research agents achieve increasingly strong benchmark scores, yet these scores do not necessarily translate into reliable delivery in ongoing research projects. Many research-agent benchmarks emphasize standalone tasks and relatively self-contained workflows in clean or curated workspaces. However, researchers ask agents to complete one step within an ongoing project, where requests depend on earlier session decisions and workspaces contain unfinished files, outdated versions, and failed attempts. We introduce ARE-bench to evaluate whether research agents advance ongoing projects while respecting prior decisions and existing workspace state, grounded in real session context and in-progress workspaces. ARE-bench includes 75 tasks built on agent sessions and full workspaces from recruited researchers' own projects, spanning seven research stages, 33 requirements, and 150 sub-requirements, with 1,173 binary checklist items in total. Each task is anchored at a real user request, preserves its requirements, and summarizes the earlier requests still in effect as background. The complete workspace is replayed to that boundary without cleanup, preserving artifacts from earlier turns. Each checklist is compiled from an intent-aligned rubric and credits any valid solution. Across seven frontier models, the strongest passes every checklist item on only 66.2% of tasks, and Design and Execution rank among the hardest stages for every model. Three models pass about 69% of tasks when only delivery contracts and general norms are checked, but just 28.4% to 40.0% once historical and material or workspace requirements are also checked. Evaluating delivery without these contextual requirements can therefore overestimate research agents and mask differences between them.

infographic.key_insight: Research-agent benchmarks can overestimate real-world ability when they ignore prior session decisions and the state of unfinished project workspaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable research agents must satisfy the current request while preserving historical constraints and working correctly with existing project artifacts.
method: Build 75 tasks from recruited researchers’ real agent sessions and full project workspaces.
Replay each workspace to a real request boundary without cleanup, retaining earlier artifacts and summarizing still-active requests.
Evaluate with intent-aligned binary checklists that credit any valid solution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven frontier models and 1,173 checklist items, the strongest model fully passed 66.2% of tasks; three models’ roughly 69% pass rates on delivery contracts and general norms fell to 28.4–40.0% when contextual requirements were included.
infographic.watch_item: The 75-task sample may not capture the full diversity of research workflows, so generalization beyond the sampled projects remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: ARE-bench: Benchmarking Agents' Research Ability in Real-World Researcher Sessions and Workspaces

title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
authors: Audrey Huang, Nan Jiang, Sham M. Kakade, Sadhika Malladi, Akshay Krishnamurthy, Dylan J. Foster
abstract: Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

infographic.key_insight: Policy optimization can suppress optimal responses even while reward improves, but periodically resetting the KL reference can preserve access to the base model’s capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory motivates combining KL regularization with reference resets to improve the sampling and optimization efficiency of language model post-training.
method: Analyze coverage collapse in REINFORCE, including with exact gradients and fixed-reference KL regularization.
Introduce Approximate Policy Mirror Descent to approximately solve successive KL-regularized subproblems with updated references.
Prove coverage-preserving guarantees for stylized PPO, GRPO, and squared-loss algorithms using softmax linear policies over pretrained features.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical failure cases and global convergence guarantees, rather than empirical benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees apply to softmax linear policies over pretrained features and stylized algorithms; they do not establish equivalent behavior for full neural-network post-training.
infographic.paper_title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets

title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
authors: Howard Zhang, Chuck Arvin, Logan Brown, Mihir Bhatia, Neelu Choudhary, Lily Miao
abstract: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.

infographic.key_insight: Trace-based evaluation best balances known-risk detection, while functional testing and security red-teaming uncover complementary failures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Pair trace-based functional evaluation with adversarial security red-teaming to assess enterprise analytics agents.
method: Compare trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics.
Evaluate two analytics agents using frozen execution traces in a controlled setting.
Measure harness stability, known-risk detection, and unknown-risk discovery across three phases.
infographic.evidence_signal: 97% of configurations met the stability threshold; on 72 ground-truth cases, trace-based judging achieved F1=0.90 while text-only judging matched recall with 5× more false alarms; discovery found 24 novel failures with no overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming.
infographic.watch_item: Results from two agents and frozen traces may not generalize to live deployments with changing tools and workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents

title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics
authors: Peng Chen, Yihang Wang, Zhongwen Rao, Yang Shu, Yuying Qiu, Yuxuan Chen
abstract: Time series analytics has been widely applied across various domains. While existing time series foundation models (TSFMs) have demonstrated promising results, they still face two major challenges: 1) Most TSFMs mainly rely on stacking Transformer layers to increase parameter size, lacking the ability to adaptively model complex time series patterns from multi-domain data. 2) Current TSFMs are primarily pre-trained for specific tasks, e.g., forecasting or anomaly detection, and a few models support multiple tasks, but they fail to fully leverage task specificity and commonality, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose TimeSeek, a novel generalized time series analytics model that adaptively models time series patterns from multi-domain data and unifies multiple tasks in pre-training. Conceptually, TimeSeek is guided by selective information sharing under domain and task heterogeneity. From the perspective of multi-domain data, we propose a Multi-Domain Feature Extractor that adaptively captures temporal dependencies and channel correlations based on domain-specific characteristics, including progressive multi-scale modeling and adaptive slot channel modeling. From the perspective of the diversity of tasks, we propose multi-task collaborative training, which leverages task specificity and task commonality through task customization and cross-task training, effectively unifying multiple tasks in pre-training and better adapting to diverse downstream scenarios. After pre-training on large-scale time series data, TimeSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification tasks across both few-shot learning and zero-shot situations, together with favorable inference efficiency.

infographic.key_insight: TimeSeek combines domain-adaptive feature extraction with multi-task pretraining to share useful information while preserving domain and task differences.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A unified model could support forecasting, anomaly detection, and classification across heterogeneous time series with limited task-specific data.
method: Progressive multi-scale modeling captures temporal dependencies.
Adaptive slot channel modeling captures domain-dependent channel correlations.
Task customization and cross-task training balance task specificity and commonality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports large-scale time series pretraining and state-of-the-art results across three tasks in few-shot and zero-shot settings, with favorable inference efficiency, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Dataset coverage, baseline comparisons, and compute requirements are unspecified in the abstract, limiting assessment of transferability and deployment cost.
infographic.paper_title: TimeSeek: Multi-Task and Multi-Domain Pretraining for Generalized Time Series Analytics

title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning
authors: Souhaila Djaffal, Amna Jamal, Gagana Madhugiri Devaraja, Anidipta Pal, Jobst Heitzig
abstract: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-generated world models can pass strict mechanical checks yet differ substantially from reference models, so executability alone does not establish fidelity to the intended decision problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Planning and verification pipelines should evaluate structural agreement and semantic fidelity alongside mechanical validity before relying on generated world models.
method: Evaluate five LLMs generating partially observable stochastic game models from natural-language scenarios.
Introduce 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings.
Assess mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria across three empirical tracks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 410 first-pass generations, the reference-backed game track yielded 134/135 mechanically valid models, but mean structural F1 was 0.366 and only 28/134 valid models exactly matched the reference.
infographic.watch_item: Multiple formalizations may be plausible, so reference mismatch alone does not prove semantic error; small automated semantic-score changes may also obscure structural shifts caused by country cues.
infographic.paper_title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

title: The Unused Input: The Initial State as a Conditioning Interface for Recurrent TSFMs
authors: Bernhard Voggenberger, Christian Ganhör, Levente Zólyomi, Sebastian Böck, Sepp Hochreiter
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast unseen series without task-specific training. Increasingly they are built on recurrent backbones, whose constant per-step cost makes long-context inference cheap, and which, unlike transformers, carry a state. A recurrent backbone computes its prediction from two inputs: the observed context window and the initial recurrent state. In practice only the first is utilised and the initial state is unused by convention. We ask whether the initial state can be utilised in recurrent TSFMs. Using the xLSTM-based zero-shot forecaster TiRex as a case study, we freeze the backbone and train only a small head that writes a context vector into the initial state, so that any change in accuracy is attributable to the injected state rather than to adapted weights. A spectral summary of the input window, learned once and applied unchanged to every series, lowers mean GiftEval MASE by 0.175%, with every seed improving, which neither a parameter-matched LoRA adapter nor a learnable static state reproduces. An embedding of text attached to each series, evaluated on six MoTime datasets, reveals two roles for the state. As a per-dataset adaptation surface, a static state lowers MASE by 0.04-6.96% of the zero-shot baseline (8-70% of the gain of full fine-tuning). As a channel for exogenous information, the text-conditioned state lowers it by a further 0.15-0.41% of the zero-shot baseline on four of six datasets and, combined with a LoRA adapter, exceeds full fine-tuning, which has no access to the text, on one of them. In TiRex, the effect concentrates in the mLSTM blocks and is strongest at short context. The results are preliminary and the improvements small, but they point to the initial state as a direction for further research.

infographic.key_insight: A recurrent forecaster’s usually unused initial state can serve as a conditioning interface, modestly improving forecasts without changing backbone weights.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Small state-writing heads offer a lightweight way to inject spectral context or series-associated text into recurrent time-series foundation models.
method: Freeze the xLSTM-based TiRex backbone and train a small head to initialize its recurrent state.
Condition the state on spectral summaries or embeddings of text attached to each series.
Compare against static states, parameter-matched LoRA adapters, and full fine-tuning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Spectral conditioning reduced mean GiftEval MASE by 0.175% across all tested seeds; on six MoTime datasets, text conditioning added reductions of 0.15–0.41% of baseline MASE on four datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Results are preliminary and TiRex-specific, with small gains concentrated in mLSTM blocks and strongest at short context.
infographic.paper_title: The Unused Input: The Initial State as a Conditioning Interface for Recurrent TSFMs

title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
authors: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang
abstract: External memory enables LLM agents to improve from experience by distilling trajectories of past tasks into concise lessons for new tasks. However, memory can also lead to memory-induced degradation, where an agent fails on tasks it would solve without memory, often because it follows a lesson that is incorrect, or misapplies or misreads a valid one. This is because lessons are inferred from trajectories labeled only with task success or failure, yet are typically provided without the trajectories they came from, leaving the agent no way to check them. To address this, we introduce WikiTrace, an evidence-linked memory system designed to let agents check each lesson against its original trajectory. Specifically, motivated by the finding that a trajectory often still holds the evidence needed to catch an erroneous lesson, WikiTrace stores each lesson as a concise insight linked to a summary of why its trajectory succeeded or failed and to the raw trajectory itself. Then, on a new task, the agent starts from all insights and, whenever one lacks details needed to act, conflicts with another, or comes from a failed task, descends through its links with terminal tools to fill in missing details or correct the insight before acting. We validate WikiTrace on five agentic benchmarks, showing that it consistently outperforms existing memory approaches and a baseline given the same insights alone, while also reducing memory-induced degradation. Our code is available at https://github.com/yukyeongleee/wikitrace

infographic.key_insight: Linking agent memory lessons to their source evidence helps prevent failures caused by incorrect, misread, or misapplied memories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent memory systems should preserve inspectable evidence alongside distilled lessons so agents can verify guidance before acting.
method: Store each concise insight with a success/failure explanation and its raw source trajectory.
Start new tasks with all insights available.
Use terminal tools to inspect linked evidence when details are missing, lessons conflict, or an insight comes from a failed task.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five agentic benchmarks, WikiTrace consistently outperformed existing memory approaches and a same-insights-only baseline while reducing memory-induced degradation.
infographic.watch_item: Preserving and inspecting raw trajectories may add storage and inference overhead; the abstract does not quantify these costs.
infographic.paper_title: Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents
